newsitem.title: USA: Clinton aide says weapons pact victim of politics.
newsitem.headline: Clinton aide says weapons pact victim of politics.

text.p: President Bill Clinton will seek Senate ratification of a treaty banning chemical weapons next year, a White House official said on Tuesday after claiming Republicans made it "a victim of partisan politics" in 1996.

Nancy Soderberg, a deputy assistant to the president for national security, also lamented that foreign policy was "a largely male preserve" but cited the nomination of Madeliene Albright as secretary of state as a step in the right direction.
Noting that foreign policy had only a limited role during the presidential campaign, Soderberg said Republicans still tried to use it for political gain.

"On the few occasions foreign policy was used to drive the public apart, the effort not only backfired from a political point of view, it jeopardised the interests of our people," she said in remarks prepared for delivery before the Women's National Democratic Club.
"During the campaign, the Chemical Weapons Convention -- long a priority of the Clinton and Bush administrations -- fell victim to partisan politics," Soderberg said.
"Short-sighted political wrangling robbed the American people of an important tool to keep weapons of mass destruction out of dangerous hands," she said.

In September, the Republican-controlled Senate failed to act on the treaty after a group of conservative Republicans led by Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina threatened to saddle it with a series of unacceptable amendments.
"This result served no one -- Republican or Democrat," Soderberg said. "President Clinton remains determined to secure ratification of this critical treaty as soon as possible."

The treaty, the result of a decade of negotiations, goes into force in April. At least 65 countries have ratified the convention, which bans the acquisition, development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons.
The accord was negotiated by Republican President George Bush and submitted to the Senate three years ago.

Conservatives said they opposed the treaty because it fails to provide protection from poison gas, would impose unacceptable new regulations on U.S. businesses and make the firms subject to unprecedented international inspections.
In her remarks to the Democratic women, Soderberg noted that "this is a promising era for women and for our nation as a whole."
"Of course, foreign policy is still a largely male preserve -- but we are making great strides," she said.
Clinton earlier this month nominated Albright, his ambassador to the United Nations, to replace Warren Christopher as secretary of state.
If confirmed by the Senate, she would be the first woman to hold the post.
